definition.text: A single linear path through a food web, usually starting with a producer such as grass or algae and ending with a top predator or decomposer.

facts.text: A food chain shows who eats whom by trophic level; a food web is the non-linear network formed when many food chains interconnect.
Its base is primary producers, which make organic compounds from sunlight or from inorganic chemicals; every other member is a consumer.
In dark places such as hydrothermal vents, chemosynthetic bacteria and archaea using hydrogen sulfide and methane form the base of the chain.
A simple example: a green plant eaten by a snail, eaten by a frog, eaten by a snake, eaten by an eagle.
When organisms die, decomposers and detritivores break their remains into simple nutrients returned to the soil for plants.
Food chains are used in ecotoxicology to trace how contaminants pass along and biomagnify.
Removing even one link can push other species toward extinction.

definition.text: The number of feeding links between a consumer and the base of its food chain.

facts.text: Generally only about ten percent of the energy at one trophic level passes to the next; the rest is used up in metabolism.
Food chains usually have no more than five trophic levels.
Eating lower in the chain gives more energy: a salad yields more energy per pound than an animal that ate lettuce.
Ecologists have proposed that chain length grows with ecosystem volume, is capped by energy loss at each level, or reflects habitat type.

definition.text: A species that plays a strong role in shaping the structure of its community.

facts.text: Foundation species can sit at any trophic level: producers, herbivores or predators.
Paul K. Dayton coined the term in 1972 for certain marine invertebrates and algae.
Corals, kelps, oysters, seagrasses, mangroves and forest trees help other organisms by creating habitat and easing physical stress such as waves and drying.
Studies removing creosote bush and eastern hemlock found species diversity rose afterwards, suggesting foundation species can sometimes limit diversity.

definition.text: A set of organisms in a community that share traits and do similar jobs, regardless of how closely related they are.

facts.text: Plant functional groups are called plant functional types; animal ones are called guilds and usually share a way of feeding.
Functional groups are identified by direct observation of behaviour and contribution, not from theory.

definition.text: The value and range of species traits that influence how an ecosystem works.

facts.text: Traits such as how an organism moves, gathers resources, reproduces or when it is active add to functional diversity.
Functional diversity raises ecosystem productivity by letting more niches be occupied.
Bees in managed landscapes show lower functional and species diversity than in natural habitats.

title: Functional redundancy

definition.text: The situation where several species in an ecosystem fill similar roles, acting as insurance if one is lost.

facts.text: A redundant species can take over the job of a similar species in the same functional niche.
Where redundancy is high, losing one species will not always reduce ecosystem function, so conserving the group matters more than any one species.
Whether conservation should protect particular species or functional traits is still debated.

contested_note: It is debated whether conserving specific species or functional traits better preserves ecosystem function.

title: Green world hypothesis

definition.text: The idea that the world stays green because predators keep down the herbivores that would otherwise eat the vegetation.

facts.text: It is also called the HSS hypothesis after Hairston, Smith and Slobodkin, who published it in 1960.
Sea otter studies support it: otters eat sea urchins, and without otters urchins nearly eliminate kelp forests, leaving urchin barrens.
The rival plant self-defense hypothesis says plants survive mainly through thorns, toxins and tough tissues.

contested_note: The plant self-defense hypothesis offers a competing explanation that plant defenses, not predators, keep herbivores from eating all vegetation.
